prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, transforming the analysis of exporting, reallocation and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: The heterogeneous-firm framework moved the unit of analysis in trade from the industry to the firm. It explains who exports, why productivity gains arise from within-industry reallocation, and why the gains from trade have a selection margin that earlier representative-firm models lacked. It also redirected empirical work toward firm-level and transaction-level data. The reach is wide: the framework carries into industrial organisation (pricing and markups under trade), macro (the productivity and reallocation channels), and development. It has more than twenty years of confirmation, and the core predictions about exporter premia and selection have held up in many countries' data. Attribution is reasonably clean for a pair. Melitz (2003) is the pivotal model. Helpman brings the monopolistic-competition foundations and, with Melitz and Yeaple, the exporting-versus-FDI extension. I keep this as a single-achievement award because pairing it with a second part would force either a fourth name or the removal of Helpman. Neither improves attribution. Maturity is not in doubt.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and overlap. The credited list omits closely related contributors, notably Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and it is unclear whether a Melitz-Helpman award would be read as underweighting them. Redding is credited on the ballot but is left out here for cleaner attribution, which is itself a judgment. Krugman's 2008 prize covers adjacent ground, so the Committee may see the area as partly rewarded. Some quantitative results, such as those relying on the Pareto form, are sensitive to functional-form assumptions. B002 drew first-place support from four members and the broadest top-three support, and I rank it a close second. My own field (international pricing and trade, plus IO) makes me more receptive to the trade case, and I should discount that.

responses.point: Teorell ranked B025 last of his eight. He sees trade as relatively recently recognised and suggests Helpman's credit may fit better under a broader trade-and-growth citation.
responses.response: I take the overlap concern seriously, but I read the 2008 prize differently. It recognised scale economies, monopolistic competition and trade patterns across countries. The Melitz mechanism concerns selection and reallocation among firms within an industry and a distinct welfare channel, and it was not covered by that prize. I agree that Helpman's work is spread over several strands. The citation can be anchored on firm heterogeneity so that his other work does not need adjudicating here. Even so, this is a real reservation. If the Committee judged that Helpman's contribution is better recognised elsewhere, I would still keep Melitz as the core and would not extend the award to others.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranked B012 first. She argues that the BLP core is a compact, well-identified three-person contribution that is both a method and a framework, and that it is used in merger review, antitrust and trade.
responses.response: I agree that B012 is strong; I put it third. The BLP trio has a cleaner attribution boundary than B025, where Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not on the ballot, and thirty years of use is persuasive. My ordering rests on a difference in kind. Melitz changed what economists think the mechanism of trade gains is, whereas BLP mainly provides a toolkit for estimating demand, which makes it a methodological contribution. That is a judgment about conceptual versus methodological weight. Since I work close to IO, I may be wrong, and I would not oppose B012 if the Committee prefers a prize built on methods that have been used across fields.

responses.point: Krusell ranked B025 third. He asks whether it is sufficiently distinct from Krugman's 2008 prize and whether the Eaton-Kortum strand should be paired with it. He also notes that Helpman's credit is divided with B029.
responses.response: I agree that the contribution is distinct from Krugman's, for the reasons given above. On Eaton-Kortum, I would keep it separate. It is a different achievement, centred on a Ricardian quantitative framework. Adding it would breach the three-person limit and blur credit. It is also not a shortlisted ballot, so it cannot be part of this configuration. On the divided credit for Helpman, I accept that B029 is not before us and I would credit him only for the firm-heterogeneity and exporting-versus-FDI work.

responses.point: Hassler ranked B002 first and proposed Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler. He centres the award on the collateral-constraint mechanism. He treats the financial-accelerator strand as limited by Bernanke's 2022 recognition. He ranked B025 second and notes that Redding is later and more derivative.
responses.response: I agree with him on Redding and on the clarity of the Kiyotaki-Moore core. On B002 I would stop at Kiyotaki and Moore. Adding Gertler runs into the 2022 overlap, and his credit is also split with the New Keynesian ballot. B002 is my strongest alternative. If the Committee preferred it, I could support it on the basis of the 1997 paper alone. The limit of three people in total means I cannot fit it alongside B025 in one configuration without dropping a name, which would cost attribution accuracy. So I present them as alternatives rather than combining them.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would regard the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as an attribution gap that undermines a Melitz-Helpman award.
How much weight the 2008 prize should carry as partial overlap, given that the selection and reallocation mechanism is distinct but the subfield is adjacent.
Whether Redding should be added or Helpman's credit narrowed. I have not verified relative contributions independently.
How sensitive the welfare and gains-from-trade conclusions are to structural and functional-form assumptions.
Whether B002 would command broader support than B025 once colleagues weigh the 2022 overlap against the 2008 overlap.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate-specific connection is apparent from the supplied profile. None of my listed co-authors is a credited name on the shortlisted ballots. My research on exchange-rate pass-through, invoicing currency and cross-border pricing is adjacent to international trade and IO, so I may be more receptive to B025 and B012. I co-authored a 2026 paper with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen, neither of whom is a candidate. My spouse is Magdalena Andersson, a public fact that has no apparent bearing on these candidates, and I do not treat it as a conflict.
